it depends on what you define as a "run."

I "run" at about 6 mph or 10:00 min/mile. Most "runners" I know have done cross country or track previously (I haven't) and they say faster than 7.5 mph is "running."

I call my outings "jogs" so as to not offend the running purists who say anything slower than a sprint is just walking.

I can "jog" at 6 mph for 6 miles consecutively, but if I'm "running" any faster than that, I can only make about 2 miles before my legs hurt.

I don't like the super high impact associated with running fast, though, so I stick to my "jogs" of 6 mph. Whatever works for you and makes you happy :-)

I typically run somewhere between 5 and 5.5 mph. If I stay at 6 mph, my heart rate hits 180-185 (I'm a mid-20's male), and that just isn't sustainable for me over a period of more than 5 or 10 minutes. I found that I can kind of pace myself based on my heart rate, aiming to keep it around 120-140, but that averages at the crossover point between walking and running.

I define running based on the biometric definition, which is basically "at some point in the stride, both feet are visibly off the ground". The Olympics uses basically this definition, as they have a speed walking event and running will get a person disqualified. Robotics also use this definition, because Honda wanted to brag that they created the first humanoid robot that could run.

If you go by this definition, then there is no lower bound in terms of speed. You can "run" in place at 0 mph.

I think it's more useful to break it down into running and jogging, like horseshatehams, so as not to offend the actual runners. Where that line is I suppose can be somewhat arbitrary. I personally draw the dividing line at a 10 minute mile, which I can barely do (but I'm getting faster with every run).
